Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. Higher temperatures are needed to achieve higher destruction efficiencies, which translates to longer heat-up times, and increased energy inputs. From a thermodynamic standpoint, the energetic requirements for SCWO are comparable to incineration of wet wastes. Under atmospheric conditions ~2600 kJ/kg of energy input is required to heat and evap - orate water from 20 ◦ C to 100 ◦ C, while heating and pressurizing water from 20 ◦ C to the supercritical phase at 25 MPa and 500 ◦ C requires ~3060 kJ/kg ( Lemmon et al., 2018 ). Under oxidizing conditions, both SCWO and incineration valorize the energetic content of the feedstock to reduce overall energy demand. SCWO does not produce particulate matter (PM), NO x or SO 2 as reaction products due to the lower operating temperatures, which eliminates the emission treatment requirements on industrial incinerators. In light of these findings, continuous SCWO processing seems more promising than batch SCWO processing as an end-of-life disposal process for PFAS-rich wastes. Continuous SCWO processing requires the PFAS to be contained in a liquid matrix with low salt content to avoid issues with scaling and corrosion.

Conclusions This study’s objective was to derive the design principles for PFAS removal using molecular dynamics simulations of six EPA-regulated PFAS compounds interacting with graphene. The simulations assessed adsorption energy, diffusion coefficients, and PFAS– graphene distances, both individually and in realistic multicomponent PFAS environments with water. The findings clearly demonstrate that graphene is a highly promising material for PFAS removal in water treatment. Higher-molecular-weight PFAS compounds exhibited stronger adsorption, with PFOS showing the highest interaction strength (500 g/mol, −171 kcal/mol). Sulfonic acid-terminated PFAS, like PFOS (−171 kcal/mol) and PFHxS (−153 kcal/mol), were adhered more strongly by graphene than carboxylate-terminated counterparts such as PFNA (−152 kcal/mol) and PFOA (−147 kcal/mol). Furthermore, graphene-enhanced PFAS diffusion in water potentially accelerates contaminant removal.
